items.excerpt: The Authors Guild is asking publishers to split Anthropic's $1.5 billion training-data settlement more fairly, noting that many houses will get large payouts while most authors get little more than 'a modest vacation'. It also warns that AI models 'continue to gorge' on books, now through destructive scanning.

Carlo Carrenho's weekly roundup: Germany's MVB is building Snackz's AI tool into its system to generate classifications, keywords and SEO copy from manuscripts or book proposals. ElredoVoice is bringing 20 HarperCollins Polska Harlequin titles into Czech audio with AI-assisted production. The roundup also looks at how AI floods pressure Amazon KDP's print-on-demand pipeline.

Spotify has widened its ElevenLabs-powered Audiobook Creation Tools beta to US self-published English-language authors. The tool turns finished EPUBs into labelled AI-narrated audiobooks with no exclusivity, in contrast to Audible's closed approach. Separately, PRH CEO Nihar Malaviya calls AI a tool for print-run and promotion decisions: 'Let AI wash the dishes so we can focus on cooking.'

Author and editor Madeleine F White argues that publishing's stance on AI is pushing writers into a culture of secrecy. If the industry wants transparency about AI use, she says, it has to make honesty safer than concealment.

Jane Friedman argues that writing conferences are failing attendees who have many practical questions about AI. She says organisers should put AI into their programming with clear intent rather than avoid it.
Lisa Cooper Ellison's craft essay on building a distinct memoir voice, a mix of natural style and sentence-level choices, before AI-assisted drafting flattens it into generic prose.

Audible UK has quadrupled its output of Audible Originals translated from European languages into English. It stresses that humans, not AI, did the translation, which sets it apart from the industry's machine-translation push.
At the Mandarin's House, a UNESCO World Heritage site, Macao poet Ng Iat-i recites 'Moon Over Lotus Isle', a Mid-Autumn poem he co-created with AI. It is a showcase for human-AI poetry collaboration.

Post-production studio Soundgrab and AI voice company Voicegrab are launching a 'hybrid cinema audiobook' format that pairs AI voice technology with film-grade sound mixing, and have hired a Hollywood re-recording mixer. The startups are tenants of Korea's NIPA Virtual Convergence Industry Hub.

Noh Seung-young, a translator with 21 years in the field, told a National Assembly Library expert panel that AI machine translation 'is not sustainable even in the short term' without human intervention. He warns that translators are being asked to do more intensive post-editing work for less pay.

Lee Sung-up, a Lezhin Comics co-founder, now runs Nautilus, maker of the children's e-book platform Ttokseo (똑서). Nautilus uses Ttokseo's reading data with generative AI to produce its own children's English content and characters as it chases a 'Disney for the AI era'.

'Grandmaslop': grandparents are using Gemini, Claude and ChatGPT to make whole personalised AI storybooks starring their grandchildren. Parents on Reddit say the books share the same slop cartoon style and stories with broken meter, a sign of how cheap AI children's-book generation is changing what counts as a picture book.
